top_papers.title: Obinutuzumab Following Rituximab Intolerance or Treatment Failure in Glomerular Disease: A Single-Centre Irish Case Series
top_papers.abstract: Obinutuzumab is a humanized type II anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody that induces more profound B-cell depletion than rituximab and has emerged as a promising therapeutic option in immune-mediated kidney disease. However, published experience in glomerular disease remains limited, particularly among patients with rituximab hypersensitivity or treatment failure. We describe 13 patients with glomerular diseases treated with obinutuzumab at a tertiary nephrology centre between 2020 and 2025, including membranous nephropathy (n=3), lupus nephritis (n=6), minimal change disease (n=2), and MPO-ANCA-associated vasculitis (n=2). Six patients had prior rituximab hypersensitivity, comprising four episodes of anaphylaxis, one episode of serum sickness, and one acute infusion reaction, and two had rituximab-refractory disease. Eleven of 13 patients achieved remission (85%), including 9 complete and 2 partial remissions. Remission was observed across all disease subtypes. Five of six lupus nephritis patients achieved remission, while all patients with minimal change disease and ANCA-associated vasculitis achieved remission. All PLA2R-positive membranous nephropathy patients achieved immunologic remission. One mild infusion reaction and one serious infection were observed. No severe infusion reactions occurred despite prior rituximab hypersensitivity. Obinutuzumab demonstrated favourable efficacy and tolerability across multiple glomerular diseases and may represent an effective alternative B-cell depleting therapy in patients with rituximab intolerance or treatment failure.
top_papers.takeaway: Obinutuzumab shows favourable efficacy and tolerability in multiple glomerular diseases, offering an effective alternative B-cell depleting therapy for patients with rituximab intolerance or treatment failure.

top_papers.title: Nephrotic syndrome in patient with hematopoietic stem cell transplant: A case report with review of literature
top_papers.abstract: Introduction: Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) is a treatment for hematopoietic malignancies and certain immune disorders. Although rare, nephrotic syndrome is a significant complication of HSCT, often linked to graft-versus-host disease (GvHD) and frequently manifesting as membranous nephropathy. This case aims to highlight the rare detection of PLA2R antibodies in a patient with nephrotic syndrome following HSCT. Case presentation: A 52-year-old man with acute myeloid leukemia underwent allogeneic HSCT. Six months after discontinuation of immunosuppressants, he experienced two episodes of GvHD, requiring further immunosuppressive therapy. One year later, he presented with lower limb edema and anorexia. Investigations revealed nephrotic-range proteinuria (24-h urine protein 13 g; urine ACR 7004 mg/g), severe hypoalbuminemia (1.97 g/dL), and hyperlipidemia. Complement levels (C3, C4) were normal. Renal biopsy demonstrated membranous nephropathy with positive anti-PLA2R staining. Treatment with corticosteroids and rituximab was initiated. The patient subsequently achieved complete remission. Literature review: A Review of 11 reported cases (mean age 53.4 years; 8 (72.7%) allogeneic, 3 (27.3%) autologous) showed membranous nephropathy as the predominant pathology (9, 81.8%), followed by minimal change disease and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (1, 9.1% each). IgG and/or C3 deposition occurred in 9 (81.8%). GvHD was present in 7 (63.6%). Treatment commonly included corticosteroids and immunosuppressants, including rituximab. Clinical improvement occurred in all cases, with complete or partial remission in 9 (81.8%). Conclusion: This case highlights the rare occurrence of nephrotic syndrome post-HSCT. The detection of anti-PLA2R antibody positivity on tissue immunofluorescence of the renal biopsy suggests a complex immune mechanism potentially overlapping with primary membranous nephropathy pathways. Corticosteroids and rituximab proved effective, reinforcing their role in management.
top_papers.takeaway: Nephrotic syndrome is a rare complication of hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, often linked to graft-versus-host disease, and can be effectively managed with corticosteroids and rituximab.

top_papers.title: A randomised controlled trial of two corticosteroid dosages for relapsed childhood steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome: the OPtimising dosE in Nephrotic syndrome (OPEN) trial protocol.
top_papers.abstract: Background Steroid sensitive nephrotic syndrome (SSNS) is a relapsing-remitting condition treated with repeated courses of high-intensity corticosteroids. Corticosteroid-related adverse effects cause morbidity and reduce quality of life. Methods The OPtimising dosE in Nephrotic syndrome (OPEN) trial is a multi-centre, randomised, controlled, non-inferiority trial comparing high-intensity with low-intensity corticosteroid treatment in children (aged 1-16 years) with relapsed SSNS. For induction, participants will receive prednisolone 60mg/m 2 (maximum 60mg) or 30 mg/m 2 (maximum 30mg) daily until remission. A second randomisation, conditional upon remission, allocates maintenance prednisolone 40mg/m 2 (maximum 40mg) or 20mg/m 2 (maximum 20mg) every other day for 4 weeks. All Australian and New Zealand tertiary paediatric nephrology centres will participate. Exclusion criteria include corticosteroid use within 14 days, familial nephrotic syndrome, or biopsy findings other than minimal change disease or focal segmental glomerulosclerosis; non-corticosteroid immunosuppression is permitted. The sample size is 330, assuming median times to remission and relapse of 9 and 100 days. The primary outcomes are time-to-remission (induction) and time-to-relapse (maintenance), analysed as the difference in restricted mean survival time (28- and 270-day horizons) with non-inferiority margins of 3 and 30 days, and power calculated assuming a true difference of zero. Randomisation (1:1) will use site-stratified, variably sized permuted blocks generated by the central trial pharmacy; participants, clinicians, site pharmacies, investigators, and data analysts will be blinded. Discussion OPEN will define the safety and efficacy of low-intensity corticosteroid treatment in relapsed SSNS; if non-inferiority is demonstrated, cumulative corticosteroid exposure could be halved. Trial registration Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry (ANZCTR) ACTRN12624001201561p. Prospectively registered on 1 October 2024.
top_papers.takeaway: Low-intensity corticosteroid treatment may be safe and effective for children with relapsed steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome, potentially halving cumulative corticosteroid exposure.

papers.title: The landscape of allele-specific expression in human kidneys
papers.abstract: Allele-specific expression (ASE), the preferential expression of one gene copy, is a key mechanism of genomic regulation. However, its role in human kidney disease remains poorly understood. In this study, we generated a high-quality, genome-wide ASE map using paired whole-genome sequencing and RNA sequencing from microdissected glomerular and tubulointerstitial compartments of patients with proteinuric kidney disease. We showed that the majority of common ASE events were deterministic and sequence-mediated. We also found that diseased kidneys exhibited significantly more ASE in glomeruli (GLOM) than tubulointerstitium (TUBE) compared to controls. Unexpectedly, higher ASE in GLOM than TUBE was significantly associated with improved kidney disease outcomes in the disease cohort. Differential gene expression analysis suggested that this was the result of an active, protective transcriptional response, including ribosome and adenosine 5'-triphosphate synthesis up-regulation, rather than pathogenic dysregulation. Our work reveals glomerular ASE as a marker of adaptive transcriptional activity in proteinuric kidney disease.
papers.takeaway: Higher allele-specific expression in glomeruli in proteinuric kidney disease patients is associated with improved kidney disease outcomes, suggesting adaptive transcriptional activity.

papers.title: Steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome due to immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated focal segmental glomerulosclerosis successfully treated with obinutuzumab
papers.abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated podocytopathies are rare but clinically relevant renal immune-related adverse events (irAEs). Herein, we describe the case of a recurrent head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) of the tongue that developed refractory nephrotic syndrome following pembrolizumab therapy. A renal biopsy showed severe injury consistent with podocytopathy likely secondary to immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) use. Management strategies typically include the use of corticosteroids and permanent discontinuation of the ICI. Despite initial improvements, the patient experienced a course of steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome (SRNS) requiring therapy with rituximab and ultimately obinutuzumab, eventually resulting in sustained remission. This case underscores the diagnostic ambiguity and management challenges of ICI-associated podocytopathy and suggests a potential role for advanced anti-CD20 therapy in refractory cases.
papers.takeaway: Immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated podocytopathy can be managed with rituximab and obinutuzumab, suggesting potential for advanced anti-CD20 therapy in refractory cases.
